1.title: Retrieval Strategies, Latency Trade-offs and Observability
1.text: Welcome to Module ten: Retrieval Strategies, Latency Trade-offs and Observability. This module covers retrieval strategies, latency trade-offs and observability. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. How to match retrieval to the data shape and the query pattern. The accuracy, latency and cost trade-off and how to justify a configuration. Observability at scale: what to log, trace and measure, and how to sample.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory Designs Search for a Retailer's Three Data Sets
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory Designs Search for a Retailer's Three Data Sets. Product manuals (long prose), order records (tables), and a code repository for the support tooling team. Questions range from "how do I reset the ice maker?" to "total returns last quarter for store twelve" to "where is the refund rule implemented?".

1.title: Retrieval Matched to Data and Query
1.text: Retrieval Matched to Data and Query. The figure shows this: Retrieval by data shape: prose uses hybrid semantic and keyword search, tables use structured queries, code uses search tools and indexes, relationships use graph or multi-hop lookups.

1.title: Retrieval Matched to Data and Query, continued
1.text: Retrieval Matched to Data and Query, continued. Long prose (manuals, policies). Query pattern: Natural-language questions. Retrieval strategy: Hybrid vector plus B M twenty-five, rerank, structure-aware chunks, citations. Identifiers and exact terms. Query pattern: Lookup by code, name, clause. Retrieval strategy: Keyword or B M twenty-five or metadata filter. Structured tables. Query pattern: Aggregation, filters, joins. Retrieval strategy: Query the database (text-to-S Q L (Structured Query Language) or a parameterized tool), not vector search. Code. Query pattern: Find definitions and usages. Retrieval strategy: Agentic search with grep or glob and file reads, or a code-embedding index. Relationships (org charts, dependencies). Query pattern: Multi-hop. Retrieval strategy: Graph queries or iterative retrieval across hops. Time-sensitive data. Query pattern: "Latest". Retrieval strategy: Metadata filters and recency weighting; freshness checks. Small fixed corpus. Query pattern: Any. Retrieval strategy: Full context with caching.

1.title: Retrieval Matched to Data and Query, continued
1.text: Retrieval Matched to Data and Query, continued. Direct lookup. Keyword or metadata filter. Vague or short. Query rewriting or expansion by the model. Multi-part or multi-hop. Decompose, retrieve per part, then combine (agentic retrieval). Needs breadth then precision. Retrieve wide, rerank, pass top K. Needs authoritative sourcing. Retrieve with metadata (source, date) and cite. Do not use vector search for aggregations. Sums, counts and joins belong in S Q L or an analytics tool; let the model write a validated, parameterized query or call a safe tool.

1.title: Retrieval Matched to Data and Query, continued
1.text: Retrieval Matched to Data and Query, continued. Agentic retrieval (the model searches iteratively) improves recall for hard questions at the price of latency and tokens; reserve it for queries that need it, and route simple lookups to a single fast search. Evaluate retrieval separately (recall@k, precision, empty-result rate) from answer quality. Exam tip: The answer follows the data shape: prose equals hybrid semantic search; exact identifiers equals keyword; tables equals structured query; code equals search tools. "Put everything in a vector store" is the distractor.

1.title: Accuracy-Latency-Cost Trade-offs
1.text: Accuracy-Latency-Cost Trade-offs. The figure shows this: The accuracy, latency and cost triangle with levers: model tier, effort, retrieval depth, reranking, caching, streaming and batch.

1.title: Accuracy-Latency-Cost Trade-offs, continued
1.text: Accuracy-Latency-Cost Trade-offs, continued. Stronger tier. Accuracy: Up. Latency: Up. Cost: Up. Higher effort or thinking. Accuracy: Up. Latency: Up. Cost: Up. More retrieved chunks or rerank. Accuracy: Up (to a point). Latency: Up. Cost: Up. Prompt caching. Accuracy: Same. Latency: Down. Cost: Down. Streaming. Accuracy: Same. Latency: Perceived latency down (time to first token). Cost: Same. Smaller tier or lower effort. Accuracy: Down. Latency: Down. Cost: Down. Routing by difficulty. Accuracy: Held. Latency: Down on average. Cost: Down. Batch A P I (application programming interface). Accuracy: Same. Latency: Much higher (not interactive). Cost: Down (fifty percent). Parallel calls. Accuracy: Same. Latency: Down (wall-clock). Cost: Same or up. Shorter output or max tokens. Accuracy: Risk if cut off. Latency: Down. Cost: Down.

1.title: Accuracy-Latency-Cost Trade-offs, continued
1.text: Accuracy-Latency-Cost Trade-offs, continued. Justify with data: measure p fifty and p ninety-five latency, time to first token, accuracy on a test set and cost per request for each configuration; choose by the client's priority (Module one). First get a prompt that works, then optimize latency; premature trimming hides what top quality looks like. Use streaming for interactive U I s, batch for non-urgent bulk, caching nearly always when a prefix repeats. Ask for sentence or paragraph limits rather than word counts when shortening output.

1.title: Observability at Scale
1.text: Observability at Scale. Observability lets you understand a running system from its outputs. For L L M (large language model) systems add content quality to the usual latency, errors and cost.

1.title: Observability at Scale, continued
1.text: Observability at Scale, continued. The figure shows this: Observability pillars: logs, traces and metrics feed dashboards, alerts and evaluation datasets.

1.title: Observability at Scale, continued
1.text: Observability at Scale, continued. Logs. What to capture: Request id (the request-id header), model, prompt version, token counts, tool calls, errors, outcome. Why: Reproduce and audit. Traces. What to capture: Per-run spans across retrieval, model calls, tools and subagents. Why: Debug non-deterministic multi-step runs. Metrics. What to capture: p fifty or p ninety-five latency, time to first token, error and retry rates, cache hit rate, cost per request, escalation rate. Why: Trends and alerts. Quality signals. What to capture: Sampled L L M-judge or human scores, thumbs, correction rates, citation validity. Why: Detect drift. Cost attribution. What to capture: Usage by workspace, A P I key, model, team. Why: Chargeback and budgets. Challenges and answers.

1.title: Observability at Scale, continued
1.text: Observability at Scale, continued. Volume. Sample detailed traces; aggregate metrics for everything. Privacy. Redact P I I in logs; content logging off by default and enabled narrowly; access controls and retention limits. Non-determinism. Log prompt version, parameters and retrieved context so a run can be replayed. Multi-step runs. Correlate with a trace id across agents and tools. Cost surprises. Per-workspace keys, usage and cost A P I s, budget alerts, cache-efficiency tracking. Metric cardinality. Limit labels; avoid unbounded values such as user ids in metric labels. Drift. Version prompts and models; compare against eval baselines after each change.

1.title: Observability at Scale, continued
1.text: Observability at Scale, continued. Anthropic usage and cost reporting (Admin A P I or analytics A P I) groups by model, workspace, A P I key, service tier, context window, data residency and speed; data appears within about five minutes; admin credentials are required. Claude Code can export Open Telemetry metrics and events (cost, tokens by type, sessions, tool decisions) to your backend; it is off until enabled, prompt text is not logged by default, and admins can set it through managed settings (Module seventeen). Alert on leading indicators: rising retry or error rates, falling cache hit rate, growing latency tail, rising escalation or thumbs-down rates. Exam tip: At scale, the right monitoring answer combines aggregate metrics, sampled traces, redacted logs and quality sampling; logging everything with full content is both costly and a privacy risk.

1.title: Observability at Scale, continued
1.text: Observability at Scale, continued. Exam tip: Choose the retrieval by data shape: prose hybrid, identifiers keyword, tables structured query, code search tools.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. By shape: Prose: hybrid plus rerank, identifiers: keyword, tables: structured query, code: search tools, relationships: iterative or graph. Never: Vector search for sums and joins. Query rewriting: For vague or short queries. Trade-offs: Tier, effort, retrieval depth, rerank up equals accuracy, latency, cost up; caching down; batch cheap but slow. Metrics: p fifty and p ninety-five latency, time to first token, cost per request, cache hit rate, errors. Observability: Logs (request id), traces, metrics, quality sampling, cost attribution. Scale: Sample traces; redact P I I; limit cardinality; alert on leading indicators. Reporting: Usage and cost by model, workspace, key; about five minutes fresh.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A retailer's users ask "total returns for store twelve last quarter" over a table of forty million order rows. Which approach fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Aggregations over structured data belong in a database query, not vector search.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A search for a specific clause number "fourteen(b)(two)" keeps returning loosely related passages. What helps most? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Exact identifiers such as clause numbers need lexical matching, which a keyword index adds to the semantic search.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A hard multi-hop question needs facts from three documents that link to each other. Which retrieval approach suits it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Iterative, agentic retrieval handles multi-hop questions, at a latency cost.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Select two. An interactive assistant must feel responsive and cost less, and quality is acceptable. Which two levers fit? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D. Streaming improves perceived latency; caching lowers time and cost.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Latency p ninety-five doubled after adding a reranking step, with quality up slightly. How should the architect decide? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Compare the measured quality gain with the latency budget and the client's priority, then tune the candidate count or reranker size.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A team logs the full prompt and response for every request in a regulated workflow. What is the better observability design? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Aggregate metrics for all traffic plus sampled, redacted traces balance debuggability against privacy, cost and retention duties.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Spend for one product line is rising unexpectedly. Which setup makes the cause easiest to find? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Attribution by workspace and key enables chargeback and investigation.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. Which metric is a leading indicator of a prompt-cache regression after a release? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A changed prefix breaks caching; the hit rate drops first.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all eight answers. Question one: B. Question two: C. Question three: B. Question four: A and D. Question five: B. Question six: C. Question seven: C. Question eight: D. In the next module, we continue the course.
